answer: Kafka's parallelism is limited by its number of partitions; for a fan-out to 10-15 million followers (e.g. a Justin Bieber post) Kafka alone is painfully slow with a limited number of partitions, and adding a large number of partitions becomes a problem of its own. Fix: club a message stream (Kafka or Kinesis) with a message broker (SQS or RabbitMQ) to get a very high degree of fan-out; per-user delivery work is handed to a queue many workers can drain (AWS: SNS topic pushing to SQS queues). One broker broadcasting is not what happens at scale. (Page note: since Kafka 4.2 share groups let consumers outnumber partitions.)
evidence: Ch4 §4.3 'How notification systems fan out': 'Kafka's parallelism is limited by its number of partitions... Kafka alone is painfully slow when you have a limited number of partitions, and adding a large number of partitions becomes a problem of its own... club a message stream (Kafka or Kinesis) with a message broker (SQS or RabbitMQ)'

answer: Every file format starts with a header identifying it. evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'On a 2xx response the browser checks the header of the bytes it got back, decides the format... invokes the matching decoder and renders the decoded image as pixels'

answer: Backend sends the image URL to the frontend, which puts it in an img tag. It returns the image to the CDN, which caches it with a TTL (e.g. about a day, usually set by Cache-Control s-maxage) and serves later requests itself; after the TTL the next request misses and the card is regenerated. answer: The database is the most brittle component of an infrastructure; whichever cloud, if the database is down everything is down. So minimise operations that lead to no state change and protect it however you can.

answer: Every write first goes to the auxiliary Redis, which checks whether the entry exists (does B already have an unread from this sender, e.g. SET B_C 1 NX). If it exists, nothing is written to main; if not, it's recorded and the write goes on to main (SADD B C). One write per sender reaches main; aux holds only existence, no counts.
evidence: Ch6 §6.2: 'Every write first goes to the auxiliary Redis, which checks whether the entry exists... If the entry exists, nothing is written to the main database. If it doesn't, the write goes on'

answer: One more network I/O per write (not much here) in exchange for preventing the main DB from going down; worth it every time. Also introduces possible inconsistency between two stores and an extra delete on clear.
evidence: Ch6 §6.2: 'It costs one more network I/O per write, and network cost is not much in this case. Preventing your main database from going down by adding a bit of network cost is a good trade-off'

answer: No check happens; all writes go to the main database, which handles the N-1 writes it handled before: the old load. The badge keeps working; aux only sheds load.
